prompt: Rafaela's five-minute comparison puts the vendor's price beside the cost of Coreto's machines. Which of the four lines is it comparing?
hint: The line that arrives as an invoice.

choices.text: Integration, the work of moving across
choices.why: Integration is hours paid once at the start; a price page does not show it.

choices.text: Operation, the hours to keep it running
choices.why: Operation is exactly what the price comparison leaves out, and it turns out to be the largest line.

choices.text: The whole TCO, since the vendor includes support
choices.why: Support in a price does not run Coreto's side; integration, operation and exit are still missing.

choices.text: Licence
choices.why: Right: the per-host and per-gigabyte price, against the machines and storage. One line of four.

prompt: The hosted service charges R$ 90 a month for each of Coreto's 60 hosts and R$ 2.50 a gigabyte for 900 GB of logs a month. What is the monthly licence, in reais?
Match each line of a total cost of ownership to when it is paid.
hint: Two are paid once, two keep going.
right_distractors: Once a year, at contract renewal

prompt: Coreto's sheet gives the self-hosted stack an integration line of zero and the hosted service R$ 48,000. Why the difference?

choices.text: The self-hosted stack is already in place and paid for
choices.why: Right: the option you have is integrated and the one you are considering is not. That asymmetry favours the incumbent.

choices.text: Open-source software needs no integration work of any kind
choices.why: A new self-hosted stack would carry an integration line too; this one is zero because it is already built.

choices.text: The vendor charges an onboarding fee for new customers
choices.why: The R$ 48,000 is Platform's own 320 hours at R$ 150, not a fee.

choices.text: Hosted dashboards are harder to build
choices.why: Difficulty is not the reason; rebuilding them is part of a move, and the self-hosted ones already exist.

prompt: Which reasons does the lesson give for operation being the line that hides? Choose all that apply.
hint: How it is spent, and where it is paid from.

choices.text: It arrives in small pieces that each look like part of the job
choices.why: Yes: an upgrade here, a night page there, and the sum is written down nowhere.

choices.text: Vendors bury it in the small print of the contract
choices.why: The large operation line here is the self-hosted one, which has no vendor contract at all.

choices.text: It is paid from headcount, which nobody reviews line by line for this decision
choices.why: Yes: the invoice goes through the licences budget, where somebody looks; salaries do not.

choices.text: It is too small to be worth measuring
choices.why: At Coreto it is 76% of the self-hosted total: the largest line, not a small one.

prompt: An engineer-year at Coreto is 1,760 hours. How many hours a year is 60% of an engineer, the self-hosted stack's operation?
In the review, a manager says: "The Platform engineers are on the payroll whatever they do, so their hours on the log store are free." What is the lesson's answer?

choices.text: Agreed, and operation should be left out of the TCO
choices.why: Leaving it out is the five-minute comparison again, and it reverses the answer.

choices.text: The salary is paid either way; the hours are spent once
choices.why: Right: an hour on the log store is an hour not spent on, for example, the on-sale load test. So it is converted at R$ 150 like any other.

choices.text: Their hours should be priced lower than R$ 150, since they are already paid
choices.why: A cheaper rate for one option's hours tilts the comparison; the lesson uses one rate for both columns.

choices.text: Hire a contractor for the stack, so the cost becomes visible
choices.why: That changes who pays, not whether the hours cost something; the TCO already makes them visible.

prompt: A colleague's sheet puts zero in the hosted service's operation line, "because the vendor runs it". What does the lesson say?
hint: Somebody at Coreto still has work to do.

choices.text: Right, since operation is the vendor's job
choices.why: The vendor runs its side. Coreto still manages the account, the agents, the access and the log volume.

choices.text: Wrong: hosted operation is larger than self-hosted
choices.why: Hosted operation is R$ 79,200 over three years against R$ 475,200 self-hosted.

choices.text: It does not matter, because the exit line covers it
choices.why: The exit is paid once, on the way out; operation is paid each month. One does not stand in for the other.

choices.text: Wrong: hosted still takes a tenth of an engineer
choices.why: Right: 176 hours a year. Zero there is the mirror image of leaving self-hosted operation out.

prompt: Over three years, hosted observability costs R$ 452,250 in total and self-hosted R$ 626,400. How much cheaper is hosted, in reais?
The sheet's last formula, =ROUND(C4/C6*100,0), returns 76. What does that number say?
hint: C4 is a line, C6 is a total.

choices.text: Operation is 76% of self-hosting
choices.why: Right: R$ 475,200 of R$ 626,400. The line nobody invoices is three quarters of that option.

choices.text: Hosted is 76% of the cost of self-hosted
choices.why: That would divide B6 by C6. C4 is the self-hosted operation line.

choices.text: The licence-only comparison was 76% wrong
choices.why: The formula reads nothing from the licence row; it divides operation by the total.

choices.text: Self-hosting is 76% more expensive
choices.why: The gap is R$ 174,150 on R$ 452,250, far less than 76%; the formula measures a share, not a gap.

prompt: Self-hosting wins only if its operation line falls by more than the R$ 174,150 gap over three years. Below how many hours a year of operation would it win, at R$ 150 an hour?
The lesson asks you to type 0 in the self-hosted integration and exit cells rather than leaving them empty. Why, when both add up the same?
hint: What does each one tell a reader?

choices.text: An empty cell makes SUM return an error
choices.why: SUM treats an empty cell as nothing to add; the total is the same.

choices.text: Zeros make the chart draw correctly
choices.why: The lesson's reason is about the reader, not the chart.

choices.text: A zero records a decision
choices.why: Right: the reader of a TCO needs to know the line was considered and judged to cost nothing.

choices.text: The finance team's template requires it
choices.why: No template is involved; the point is what the cell says to whoever reviews the decision.

prompt: Coreto's sheet gives the self-hosted stack no integration and no exit, both of which favour it, and hosted still wins. How does the lesson read that?
hint: Which way do the errors run?

choices.text: The sheet is biased towards one side and should be redone before deciding
choices.why: Redoing it would add cost to self-hosted and widen the gap; the decision would not move.

choices.text: The conclusion is strong: it survives assumptions against it
choices.why: Right: and saying so in the recommendation tells the reader which way the errors run.

choices.text: Hosting wins by luck, and the margin is meaningless
choices.why: The margin is R$ 174,150 after two simplifications against hosted: the opposite of luck.

choices.text: Integration and exit cancel out, so they are left out
choices.why: They do not cancel: both are zero on one side and positive on the other.

prompt: Asked why the exit line is blank, a team answers: "We are not planning to leave." What does the lesson say is wrong with that answer?
hint: Nobody plans to leave on the day they sign.

choices.text: It confuses a plan to leave with a price for leaving
choices.why: Right: companies leave anyway, and the cost of leaving was set by decisions made while integrating.

choices.text: The team should be planning to leave from day one
choices.why: The lesson asks for a price, not for a plan to leave. Pricing it is compatible with staying.

choices.text: The exit belongs in a separate risk register, not in the TCO
choices.why: The exit is the fourth line of the TCO in this lesson; moving it elsewhere is how it gets forgotten.

choices.text: Leaving is free if the contract is monthly
choices.why: A monthly contract removes a notice period, not the 280 hours of moving dashboards, alerts and agents.

prompt: Leaving the hosted service takes 280 hours at R$ 150, plus one month of the R$ 7,650 licence while both run. What is the exit, in reais?
Which choices made during integration make Coreto's exit from the hosted service cheaper? Choose all that apply.
hint: What would have to be redone on the way out?

choices.text: Instrumenting the services with a vendor-neutral library
choices.why: Yes: services keep their instrumentation when the vendor changes.

choices.text: Writing the alerts in the vendor's own query language
choices.why: That is what makes the exit dearer: each alert has to be rewritten on the way out.

choices.text: Keeping dashboards and alert rules as files in a repository
choices.why: Yes: the inventory exists outside the vendor, ready to move.

choices.text: Signing a longer contract for a discount
choices.why: A longer term adds a contract lock-in; it makes leaving dearer, not cheaper.

prompt: By the lesson, Coreto's leverage over data export and notice periods is greatest before it ___ the contract.
hint: The day the deal is won.

prompt: Put the four lines of Coreto's hosted option in order of size over three years, largest first.
trap: The exit is easy to put last because it is paid once, at the end, but at R$ 49,650 it is larger than the R$ 48,000 integration.

prompt: Another company compares a hosted CI service, priced per build minute, with running its own build servers, priced at what the machines cost. Which line is most likely to change the answer?
hint: Who keeps the build servers alive?

choices.text: Licence, since build minutes add up
choices.why: Licence is the line already being compared; the question is what the comparison is missing.

choices.text: Exit, since build pipelines are hard to move
choices.why: The exit matters and belongs in the sheet, but the line that reversed Coreto's answer was larger and recurring.

choices.text: Operation of the self-run build servers
choices.why: Right: upgrades, capacity, the night page when builds queue. The line nobody invoices, as at Coreto.

choices.text: Integration of the hosted service, since it is one-off
choices.why: One-off work is paid once; a recurring line over three years outgrows it, as Coreto's sheet shows.

prompt: TCO stands for total cost of ___.
hint: Having it, from entry to exit.

prompt: Rafaela's recommendation ends: "Platform's freed hours go to the on-sale load test." Why does the lesson say that sentence matters as much as the numbers?
hint: When is a saved hour a saving?

choices.text: It makes the CFO approve the licence faster
choices.why: Speed of approval is not the point; the sentence is about what the saving consists of.

choices.text: It names where the hours go
choices.why: Right: naming the work — here one of lesson 1's four actions — is what makes the money real.

choices.text: It shows the Platform team agreed with the decision
choices.why: Agreement is welcome, but the sentence matters because it says where the hours go.

choices.text: It replaces the exit line in the recommendation
choices.why: The exit is priced separately; this sentence is about the operation hours that hosting frees.
